title: In-memory key-value store with TTL
scopeHtml:
Scope: key-value store with lazy and active TTL expiry, injectable clock, ConcurrentHashMap version.

Scope: key-value store with lazy and active TTL expiry, injectable clock, ConcurrentHashMap version.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
Design an in-memory key-value store (a mini Redis) with optional per-key TTL: put, put with TTL, get, delete, and expired keys must disappear.

Clarify:

  • Functional: put, put with TTL, get returns null if missing or expired, delete.
  • Rules: TTL 0 or none means never expires; a plain put clears an old TTL.
  • Out of scope: persistence, eviction by memory (LRU), clustering.
  • Scale talk: Redis serves on the order of 100,000 operations per second per core with sub-millisecond latency; its expiry uses both lazy and active strategies, exactly what we build.

Worked example. Clock at 1000 ms. put b "2" ttl 500 expires at 1500; put c "3" ttl 100 expires at 1100. At 1200: c is gone (null), b still 2. At 1600 a sweep removes b; one permanent key a remains.

Industry examples. Redis: lazy expiry on access plus an active cycle that samples keys with TTLs about 10 times a second and removes expired ones (confirm in the Redis docs). Memcached expires lazily and by LRU. DynamoDB TTL deletes in the background within a delay window.

Everyday analogy. Milk in a fridge: you notice it is off when you reach for it (lazy), and now and then you clean out the shelf (sweep).

Common interview traps.

  • Starting one timer thread per key (millions of threads).
  • Calling System.currentTimeMillis() directly, making tests slow or flaky.

notes.title: Core entities
notes.html:
• Entry: value and expiresAt (0 = never).
  • KVStore: the map and the operations.
  • clock: a LongSupplier injected so tests control time.

Decision gravity. Injecting the clock is a tiny cost now and makes every TTL test instant and deterministic. Reversible: yes, but retrofitting it into code full of direct System.currentTimeMillis() calls is annoying. Store an absolute expiresAt, not a remaining duration, so nothing needs decrementing.

Everyday analogy. A date stamped on the packaging instead of a countdown.

Common interview traps.

  • Storing a relative TTL and trying to update it every second.
  • Using wall-clock time for TTLs in a real service; prefer a monotonic clock (System.nanoTime) because wall time can jump.

notes.title: Class diagram
notes.html:
+--------------------------+     +-------------------------+
| KVStore                  | *   | Entry (record)         |
| map: Map<String,Entry>   |---->| value                  |
| clock: LongSupplier      |     | expiresAt (0 = never)  |
| put(k,v)  put(k,v,ttl)   |     +-------------------------+
| get(k)    delete(k)      |
| sweep()   size()         |
+--------------------------+

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing the sweep timer into the store instead of calling sweep() from outside.

notes.title: Key patterns
notes.html:
• Lazy expiration: check on get and remove if expired. Zero background cost; cold expired keys linger and hold memory.
  • Active expiration: periodic sweep() removes cold expired keys. Alternative: a min-heap (or DelayQueue) keyed by expiresAt, so the sweeper only touches due keys in O(log n) instead of scanning everything. Redis samples random keys instead of keeping a full index.
  • Dependency injection of the clock (a form of Strategy).
  • Not used: Singleton, Observer. Add an eviction listener only when asked.

Worked example. 1M keys, 10% with TTL, sweep every 1 s scanning all: 1M checks per second, wasteful. With a heap of the 100k TTL keys, a sweep only pops the few that are due. Memory cost: 100k heap entries, around a few MB.

Industry examples. Redis (lazy plus sampled active), Caffeine cache (timer wheel), Guava cache (expiry on access/write).

Everyday analogy. Supermarket staff scanning every item daily versus checking only the shelf-front items due that day.

Common interview traps.

  • Choosing only lazy and forgetting the memory leak of never-read keys.
  • Choosing only active and returning stale values between sweeps.

notes.title: Code
notes.html:
import java.util.*;
import java.util.function.LongSupplier;

class KVStore {
    private record Entry(String value, long expiresAt) {}   // 0 = never expires
    private final Map<String, Entry> map = new HashMap<>();
    private final LongSupplier clock;                        // injectable for tests
    KVStore(LongSupplier clock) { this.clock = clock; }

    void put(String k, String v) { map.put(k, new Entry(v, 0)); }
    void put(String k, String v, long ttlMs) { map.put(k, new Entry(v, clock.getAsLong() + ttlMs)); }

    String get(String k) {
        Entry e = map.get(k);
        if (e == null) return null;
        if (e.expiresAt() != 0 && e.expiresAt() <= clock.getAsLong()) { map.remove(k); return null; } // lazy expiry
        return e.value();
    }
    boolean delete(String k) { return map.remove(k) != null; }

    int sweep() {                                            // active expiry, call from a timer
        long now = clock.getAsLong(); int n = 0;
        for (Iterator<Map.Entry<String, Entry>> it = map.entrySet().iterator(); it.hasNext();) {
            Entry e = it.next().getValue();
            if (e.expiresAt() != 0 && e.expiresAt() <= now) { it.remove(); n++; }
        }
        return n;
    }
    int size() { return map.size(); }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        long[] now = {1000};
        KVStore s = new KVStore(() -> now[0]);
        s.put("a", "1"); s.put("b", "2", 500); s.put("c", "3", 100);
        now[0] += 200;
        System.out.println(s.get("c") + " " + s.get("b") + " " + s.get("a"));   // null 2 1
        now[0] += 400;
        System.out.println("swept " + s.sweep() + " left " + s.size());          // swept 1 left 1
        if (s.get("b") != null || !"1".equals(s.get("a"))) throw new AssertionError();
    }
}

Kotlin core:

class KVStore(private val clock: () -> Long) {
    private data class Entry(val value: String, val expiresAt: Long)   // 0 = never
    private val map = HashMap<String, Entry>()

    fun put(k: String, v: String, ttlMs: Long = 0) {
        map[k] = Entry(v, if (ttlMs > 0) clock() + ttlMs else 0)
    }
    fun get(k: String): String? {
        val e = map[k] ?: return null
        if (e.expiresAt != 0L && e.expiresAt <= clock()) { map.remove(k); return null }
        return e.value
    }
    fun delete(k: String) = map.remove(k) != null
    fun sweep(): Int {
        val now = clock()
        val before = map.size
        map.values.removeIf { it.expiresAt != 0L && it.expiresAt <= now }
        return before - map.size
    }
}

Common interview traps.

  • Off by one: a key is expired when expiresAt <= now; decide and test the boundary.

notes.title: Run and test
notes.html:
javac -d out Main.java
java -cp out Main
null 2 1
swept 1 left 1

Test: expiry boundary, overwrite resets TTL, plain put removes TTL, delete of an expired key, sweep count, large key counts.

Common interview traps.

  • Using Thread.sleep in tests instead of the fake clock.

notes.title: Concurrency
notes.html:
The simple version uses a plain HashMap; concurrent put and sweep can corrupt it or throw ConcurrentModificationException. Also get is a read that sometimes writes (lazy removal), so it is not a pure read.

Thread-safe version. Use ConcurrentHashMap and make each key operation atomic with its compute methods; the sweeper runs on a daemon scheduler.

class ConcurrentKVStore {
    private record Entry(String value, long expiresAt) {}
    private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, Entry> map = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final LongSupplier clock;
    private final ScheduledExecutorService sweeper = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor(r -> {
        Thread t = new Thread(r, "kv-sweeper"); t.setDaemon(true); return t; });

    ConcurrentKVStore(LongSupplier clock) {
        this.clock = clock;
        sweeper.scheduleWithFixedDelay(this::sweep, 1, 1, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
    }
    void put(String k, String v, long ttlMs) {
        map.put(k, new Entry(v, ttlMs > 0 ? clock.getAsLong() + ttlMs : 0));
    }
    String get(String k) {
        Entry e = map.get(k);
        if (e == null) return null;
        if (e.expiresAt() != 0 && e.expiresAt() <= clock.getAsLong()) {
            map.remove(k, e);                 // removes ONLY if still this exact entry; a fresh put wins
            return null;
        }
        return e.value();
    }
    int sweep() {
        long now = clock.getAsLong(); int n = 0;
        for (var en : map.entrySet())
            if (en.getValue().expiresAt() != 0 && en.getValue().expiresAt() <= now
                && map.remove(en.getKey(), en.getValue())) n++;
        return n;
    }
}

The crucial detail is the two-argument remove(key, value): if another thread overwrote the key with a fresh value just after we saw the expired one, a plain remove(key) would delete the new, valid entry. The conditional remove is a compare-and-delete.

Production note (gravity). Redis avoids all of this by being single-threaded for commands (one thread owns the data, no locks); that choice trades multi-core write throughput for simplicity and predictable latency, and you scale by running many shards. Memory cap and eviction (LRU/LFU) come next and are a policy decision you cannot easily reverse once clients depend on it (Redis maxmemory-policy).

Common interview traps.

  • Using synchronized on every method and calling it done; correct but a global bottleneck.
  • Plain remove(key) in the lazy path (race above).
  • Scanning with a stale snapshot and deleting a refreshed key.

notes.title: Follow-ups
notes.html:
• Eviction when memory is full: LRU (linked hash map) or LFU; interacts with TTL.
  • Heap or timing wheel for O(log n) expiry instead of scanning.
  • INCR, lists, hashes: more value types behind an interface.
  • Persistence: append-only log plus snapshots (Redis AOF/RDB).
  • Sharding with consistent hashing (see the HLD track).

Common interview traps.

  • Not saying what happens to TTLs on restart (stored as absolute timestamps, so they survive).

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Entry holds value plus absolute expiresAt; clock is injected.
  • Lazy expiry on read plus periodic sweep; heap or wheel when the key count is big.
  • Boundary rule: expired when expiresAt <= now.
  • Concurrent version: ConcurrentHashMap, conditional remove(key, value), daemon sweeper.
  • Redis picks single-threaded commands; know the trade-off.

questions.promptHtml: How does a key-value store with TTL make expired keys disappear? Compare lazy and active expiration.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The central design choice of the problem, with a memory-versus-correctness trade-off.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Lazy expiry checks the key on get and removes it if past its time: zero background cost, and the caller never sees a stale value, but keys that are never read stay in memory forever. Active expiry runs a periodic sweep() that removes expired keys, which bounds memory but is stale until the next sweep if used alone. A real store uses both, as Redis does: lazy on access plus a sampled background cycle.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
get(k) -> entry? -> expiresAt != 0 && expiresAt <= now ?  yes: remove, return null
timer  -> sweep() -> remove all with expiresAt <= now

Scanning every key each second is O(N) per sweep: 1M keys means 1M checks per second. Better: a min-heap or timing wheel keyed by expiresAt so the sweeper only touches due keys in O(log n), or Redis-style random sampling.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
if (e.expiresAt() != 0 && e.expiresAt() <= clock.getAsLong()) { map.remove(k); return null; }
if (e.expiresAt != 0L && e.expiresAt <= clock()) { map.remove(k); return null }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Only lazy: memory leak for write-once keys.
  • Only active: stale reads between sweeps.
  • A timer thread per key (millions of threads).
  • Boundary: decide expired when expiresAt <= now and test it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How often should the sweeper run? -> Trade CPU vs memory: 100 ms to 1 s with a time budget per run.
  2. What does Redis do? -> Samples keys with TTLs repeatedly and deletes expired ones; repeats if many were expired (verify exact parameters in docs).
  3. Why heap or wheel? -> Avoid scanning non-expiring or far-future keys.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "check on read". Senior says why both are needed, quantifies the sweep cost, and names the heap/wheel/sampling options.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A session store relied only on lazy expiry; keys for users who never came back filled the heap over weeks.

questions.promptHtml: Why store expiresAt as an absolute time and inject the clock instead of calling the system clock directly?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks testability and time-handling judgement, a frequent source of production bugs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An absolute expiresAt needs no updating: expiry is a single comparison with now, whereas a stored remaining TTL would have to be decremented continuously. Injecting a LongSupplier clock lets tests move time by assigning a variable, with no sleeps. For real services, wall time can jump (NTP, manual change), so for relative TTLs a monotonic clock like System.nanoTime is safer; wall-clock is needed only when expiry must be shared across machines or persisted.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
put(k,v,ttl=500) at t=1000 -> expiresAt = 1500
at t=1200: 1500 <= 1200 ? no -> alive
at t=1600: 1500 <= 1600 ? yes -> expired

Persistence: absolute wall-clock timestamps survive a restart (a key with 10 minutes left has about 10 minutes left after reload), while a monotonic reading is meaningless in another process.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
long[] now = {1000};
KVStore s = new KVStore(() -> now[0]);
s.put("c", "3", 100);
now[0] += 200;                       // time travel
assert s.get("c") == null;
var now = 1000L
val s = KVStore { now }
s.put("c", "3", 100)
now += 200                           // time travel
check(s.get("c") == null)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Remaining-TTL counters updated by a timer.
  • System.currentTimeMillis() scattered through the class.
  • Using wall time for in-process timeouts and being hit by clock adjustments.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can't you use nanoTime for persisted TTLs? -> Its origin is arbitrary per JVM.
  2. TTL 0? -> Convention: no expiry; a plain put clears an old TTL.
  3. Does the clock need to be thread-safe? -> The supplier is called from many threads; keep it a pure read.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "so tests are easy". Senior adds wall vs monotonic, persistence meaning and what a plain put does to an existing TTL.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A leap-second and a bad NTP step made keys expire an hour early on one cluster because TTLs used wall time.

questions.contextHtml:
A Kotlin rewrite is released. Reports: "session never expires after I refresh it with a plain put"; "keys live one millisecond too long"; "after delete and re-put the value comes back".

Languages: Kotlin · Java
class KVStore(private val clock: () -> Long) {
    private val map = HashMap<String, String>()
    private val expiry = HashMap<String, Long>()

    fun put(k: String, v: String, ttlMs: Long = 0) {
        map[k] = v
        if (ttlMs > 0) expiry[k] = clock() + ttlMs
    }
    fun get(k: String): String? {
        val exp = expiry[k]
        if (exp != null && exp < clock()) { map.remove(k); return null }
        return map[k]
    }
    fun delete(k: String) { map.remove(k) }
}
class KVStore {
    private final Map<String,String> map = new HashMap<>();
    private final Map<String,Long> expiry = new HashMap<>();
    void put(String k, String v, long ttlMs) {
        map.put(k, v);
        if (ttlMs > 0) expiry.put(k, clock.getAsLong() + ttlMs);
    }
    String get(String k) {
        Long exp = expiry.get(k);
        if (exp != null && exp < clock.getAsLong()) { map.remove(k); return null; }
        return map.get(k);
    }
    boolean delete(String k) { return map.remove(k) != null; }
}
questions.promptHtml: Find all defects and propose a structure that prevents them.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Fixes < to <= and nothing else.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Should a plain put clear the TTL (spec says yes)? Is a key expired at expiresAt exactly?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Patch the three bugs; the structure change follows.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) put without TTL does not remove the old expiry entry, so a permanent write inherits an old TTL, or (worse for the report) a refresh keeps an earlier expiry; (b) < should be <=: at exactly expiresAt it must be expired; (c) delete removes the value but leaves the expiry entry, so a later plain put is expired immediately or inherits the old time; (d) expired keys removed from map but expiry entry stays: a leak.
  4. How I'd verify each: Table-driven tests: put with TTL then plain put; boundary at exactly expiresAt; delete then re-put; size of both maps.
  5. Root cause: Two parallel maps hold facts about one key, so every operation must update both and one forgets.
  6. Fix: One map from key to Entry(value, expiresAt); put always replaces the entry, so TTL state can never go stale; delete removes one entry.
Languages: Java · Kotlin
private record Entry(String value, long expiresAt) {}
void put(String k, String v) { map.put(k, new Entry(v, 0)); }
void put(String k, String v, long ttl) { map.put(k, new Entry(v, clock.getAsLong() + ttl)); }
private data class Entry(val value: String, val expiresAt: Long)
fun put(k: String, v: String, ttlMs: Long = 0) {
    map[k] = Entry(v, if (ttlMs > 0) clock() + ttlMs else 0)
}
  1. Prevention: Make illegal states unrepresentable (single entry); boundary and delete tests.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: One entry costs an extra object per key; worth it. I would not patch with more cleanup code.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Should put with an existing key and no TTL clear the TTL? -> Spec: yes. Redis SET clears TTL; SET ... KEEPTTL keeps it (verify in docs).
  • Negative TTL? -> Reject or treat as already expired; state the choice.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A cache with separate value and expiry maps leaked expiry entries for deleted keys and grew to gigabytes unnoticed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only fixes <.
  • Hire: finds the stale expiry state in put/delete.
  • Strong hire: collapses state into one entry and writes boundary tests.

questions.contextHtml: Operations: the store must not exceed 1M entries; when full, drop the least recently used key. Keys also have TTLs. A developer adds an LinkedHashMap with accessOrder=true and removeEldestEntry, then notices that expired keys occupy slots while live keys are evicted.
questions.promptHtml: How do eviction and expiry interact, and how do you structure the change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Replaces the map with an LRU and forgets expiry, or evicts live keys while stale ones remain.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: LRU or LFU? Is the capacity by count or bytes? Is concurrent access needed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Before evicting a live key, drop any expired ones found.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Options: (a) LRU only; (b) LRU plus prefer evicting expired; (c) separate expiry structure so expired entries are found in O(log n).
  4. How I'd verify each: Test: fill to capacity with half expired and add a key; no live key may be evicted.
  5. Root cause: Two policies (expire and evict) compete for the same slots; expiry must have priority because an expired key is dead weight.
  6. Fix: On insert when at capacity: first sweepSome() using a heap of expiries to pop due keys; if still full, evict the LRU. Access order updates on get mean get is a write to the structure (needs a lock or per-segment structure in the concurrent version).
Languages: Java · Kotlin
class LruStore extends LinkedHashMap<String, Entry> {
    final int cap;
    LruStore(int cap) { super(16, 0.75f, true); this.cap = cap; }
    protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<String, Entry> e) { return size() > cap; }
}
class LruStore(private val cap: Int) : LinkedHashMap<String, Entry>(16, 0.75f, true) {
    override fun removeEldestEntry(e: MutableMap.MutableEntry<String, Entry>) = size > cap
}
  1. Prevention: Test combos: expired over capacity, refresh via get changes LRU order, TTL plus eviction counters exposed as metrics.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Redis chooses approximate LRU by sampling to avoid per-access bookkeeping (verify in docs). The eviction policy is hard to reverse once clients rely on it, so I document it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Thread safety of the LinkedHashMap version? -> Not thread-safe, and access-order get mutates; wrap in a lock or use Caffeine.
  • Evict by bytes? -> Track approximate size per entry and evict until under the budget.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An LRU in front of a database evicted live hot keys because 30% of slots held expired entries nobody had swept.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: LRU only.
  • Hire: expiry first, then LRU.
  • Strong hire: thread-safety of access order, approximate LRU idea, metrics.

questions.subtopic: TTL tests with a fake clock
questions.contextHtml: The existing tests use Thread.sleep(1100) to wait for a 1 s TTL; there are 40 such tests and the suite takes 70 s. A colleague wants to "mock System.currentTimeMillis with PowerMock".
questions.promptHtml: How do you make TTL logic testable, and which cases do you cover?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Mocks static methods or reduces TTL to 10 ms.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can we change the constructor? Does the sweeper thread run in tests?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a clock parameter with the default System::currentTimeMillis.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Real time makes tests slow and flaky; static mocking is fragile and global.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run the suite: sleeps should disappear and runtime fall to milliseconds.
  5. Root cause: An implicit dependency on the system clock.
  6. Fix: Constructor-injected LongSupplier; tests advance a variable. The sweeper's schedule is not tested by sleeping: call sweep() directly.
Languages: Java · Kotlin
long[] now = {1000};
KVStore s = new KVStore(() -> now[0]);
s.put("b", "2", 500);
now[0] = 1499; assert "2".equals(s.get("b"));   // alive 1ms before
now[0] = 1500; assert s.get("b") == null;        // boundary: expired AT expiresAt
var now = 1000L
val s = KVStore { now }
s.put("b", "2", 500)
now = 1499; check(s.get("b") == "2")
now = 1500; check(s.get("b") == null)
  1. Prevention: Cases: boundary at expiresAt-1, expiresAt; overwrite resets TTL; plain put removes TTL; delete of an expired key returns false; sweep returns the count and leaves live keys; clock moving backwards does not resurrect keys (state the intended behaviour).
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No static mocking and no sleeps. One test with the real clock and a generous bound to prove wiring.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Test the concurrent version deterministically? -> Fake clock plus a latch-driven interleaving, plus a stress test for invariants.
  • Clock goes backwards? -> A key past its expiry may become valid again if you only compare; a monotonic clock avoids that.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Cutting TTL tests from 70 s to 0.3 s let the team run them on every commit and catch an off-by-one in expiry boundary.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: sleeps or static mocks.
  • Hire: injected clock, boundary tests.
  • Strong hire: backwards clock behaviour, sweep count, concurrent test approach.

questions.contextHtml:
The team moved to a ConcurrentHashMap and kept lazy expiry:

Languages: Java · Kotlin
String get(String k) {
    Entry e = map.get(k);
    if (e == null) return null;
    if (e.expiresAt() != 0 && e.expiresAt() <= clock.getAsLong()) {
        map.remove(k);               // plain remove
        return null;
    }
    return e.value();
}
fun get(k: String): String? {
    val e = map[k] ?: return null
    if (e.expiresAt != 0L && e.expiresAt <= clock()) {
        map.remove(k)                // plain remove
        return null
    }
    return e.value
}

In production, users randomly lose freshly written values: write latency looks fine, but a read right after put sometimes returns null and the key is gone afterwards. Rate: about 1 in 50,000 reads under heavy traffic.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the race and fix both get and the sweeper.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "ConcurrentHashMap is thread-safe, so it must be something else" or wraps everything in synchronized.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are there concurrent writers to the same key? Is the sweeper also running? Is the read path hot?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Switch to the two-argument remove(key, value).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Check-then-act: T1 reads the expired entry E1, T2 puts a fresh E2, T1 calls remove(k) and deletes E2; (b) same race in the sweeper iterating a snapshot; (c) clock skew is a red herring.
  4. How I'd verify each: Stress test: one thread puts a fresh value in a loop while another reads expired entries; assert a just-put value is never lost.
  5. Root cause: The decision (this entry is expired) is made on one entry, but the action (remove(k)) targets whatever entry is now under the key. Each call is atomic; the pair is not.
  6. Fix: Compare-and-delete: remove only if the mapping is still the expired entry we saw.
Languages: Java · Kotlin
if (expired(e)) { map.remove(k, e); return null; }       // removes ONLY if still this entry
int sweep() {
    long now = clock.getAsLong(); int n = 0;
    for (var en : map.entrySet())
        if (expired(en.getValue(), now) && map.remove(en.getKey(), en.getValue())) n++;
    return n;
}
if (expired(e)) { map.remove(k, e); return null }
fun sweep(): Int {
    val now = clock(); var n = 0
    for ((k, v) in map) if (expired(v, now) && map.remove(k, v)) n++
    return n
}

remove(key, value) uses equals; with a record of (value, expiresAt) two entries equal in content are interchangeable, which is harmless. Use an identity-based wrapper if that matters. 7. Prevention: The stress test in CI; review rule "check-then-act on a concurrent map needs a compound method (compute, conditional remove)". 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: synchronized on every method is correct but a global bottleneck; compare-and-delete keeps reads lock-free.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not computeIfPresent in get? -> It would work and be atomic per key, but takes a bin lock even on non-expired reads; the CAS-style remove only costs on the expiry path.
  • Is put racing with the sweeper safe? -> Yes with conditional remove; the fresh entry survives.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A cache lost 0.002% of fresh writes for months; it looked like network errors until a stress test showed the delete-the-new-entry race.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: denies a race exists.
  • Hire: conditional remove in get.
  • Strong hire: also the sweeper, equals semantics, and a stress test.

questions.contextHtml: A store has 50M keys, 5M with TTLs. The sweeper runs every second doing a full entrySet() scan under a global lock. Metrics: get p99 jumps from 0.4 ms to 900 ms every second on a metronome, one core pegged for about 800 ms of each second, heap 14 GB, expired-but-present keys at any time about 1.2M. Red herring: GC pauses are only 30 ms.
questions.promptHtml: Why does latency spike every second, and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Slow the sweeper to every 10 s, which makes the spike rarer and bigger.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the lock held during the whole scan? What staleness is acceptable? Do TTLs cluster at the same instant (a batch of sessions created together)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Bound each sweep by a time budget (say 5 ms) and resume from a cursor next tick.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) a full scan of 50M entries takes about 800 ms and holds the lock, blocking reads; (b) the work is proportional to all keys, though only 5M have TTLs and few are due; (c) a synchronised expiry wave (all TTLs 1 h from a batch).
  4. How I'd verify each: Sweep duration metric, lock hold time, histogram of TTL expiresAt buckets.
  5. Root cause: The sweeper's cost depends on N, not on the number of due keys, and it runs inside a global critical section.
  6. Fix: Keep a separate structure only for TTL keys: min-heap (or timing wheel) of (expiresAt, key); sweeper pops entries with expiresAt <= now, validates against the map with conditional remove, in bounded batches of a few thousand. Or Redis-style sampling: test 20 random TTL keys, repeat while more than 25% are expired (verify exact numbers). Add jitter to TTL values to avoid synchronised waves.
  7. Prevention: Metric for sweep duration and expired-but-resident ratio; load test with synchronized expiries.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The heap costs memory (5M entries x tens of bytes) and a duplicate stale entry when a key is overwritten (skip on validation). Sampling gives probabilistic cleanup, never exact.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Key overwritten with a longer TTL; the heap still has the old entry? -> Validate against the current entry when popped; ignore if not expired.
  • Memory of heap too large? -> Wheel with coarse 1 s buckets.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A once-a-minute full scan caused a metronomic latency sawtooth that dashboards averaged away; p99 charts revealed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: lengthens the interval.
  • Hire: bounded work, heap or wheel.
  • Strong hire: validates on pop, jitter for waves, and chooses metrics to prove it.

questions.contextHtml: You are asked to scale the store from 40,000 to 400,000 ops/s on a 16-core box and survive restarts with TTLs intact. Candidates: (A) ConcurrentHashMap with a thread pool, (B) a single-threaded command loop like Redis with one shard per core (16 shards, routed by hash(key)), (C) a global synchronized. The business can tolerate losing the last second of writes.
questions.promptHtml: Pick one, justify with trade-offs, and describe persistence and TTL behaviour on restart.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Picks (A) because it is "more parallel" without discussing compound operations, or says (C) is fine.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Operation mix (reads vs writes)? Need multi-key transactions or atomic INCR? Value sizes? Is one-second durability loss really fine?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (design); I would measure before choosing: single-thread throughput of simple ops is often hundreds of thousands per second, so (C) may fail on contention, not on raw speed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (A) gives parallel reads, but every compound operation (INCR, check-expire-then-delete) needs per-key atomic compute methods and the sweeper races with writers; (B) removes locks within a shard and makes compound ops trivially atomic, at the cost of cross-shard operations and head-of-line blocking from a slow command; (C) serialises everything.
  4. How I'd verify each: Benchmark with the real mix; test p99 with a few slow commands present.
  5. Root cause (of the trade): Locks cost contention and complexity; single-threaded shards cost routing and cross-shard atomicity.
  6. Fix: I choose (B): 16 shards, each owning its map, expiry heap and an append-only log; a request is routed to its shard's queue. Persistence: append-only log of writes (with absolute expiresAt timestamps) fsynced about every second plus periodic snapshots; on restart load snapshot, replay log, then lazy expiry removes anything past its time. Because TTLs are absolute wall-clock times, downtime counts toward expiry.
  7. Prevention: Soak test with kill -9 during writes; test restart with expired and live keys; monitor per-shard queue depth.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use a monotonic clock for persisted expiry. Choosing the persistence model (log fsync policy) is hard to reverse once clients assume durability, so I would document it. Multi-key operations across shards need either hash tags to co-locate keys or are unsupported.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• One hot key? -> It lives on one shard and caps at one core; replicate reads or cache locally.
  • Rehashing shard count later? -> Needs a migration; consistent hashing reduces the moved data (see the HLD track).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team added a global lock "temporarily" to an in-memory store; it capped at 30,000 ops/s and every later feature added more work inside that lock.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: global lock or unexplained choice.
  • Hire: compares A and B with compound-operation and sweeper concerns.
  • Strong hire: persistence with absolute TTLs, replay semantics, hot-key and cross-shard limits.
